name: Dog First Aid Checklist
description: A dog-specific checklist to help owners respond to choking, bleeding, heatstroke, and paw injuries and know when to call the vet.

items.text: Save your vet and nearest emergency hospital numbers
Keep a pet poison helpline number handy
Stock and check a dog first aid kit
Learn your dog's normal breathing and gum color
Keep a leash, towel, and carrier accessible
items.note: Program emergency numbers into your phone in advance

items.text: Look for pawing at the mouth, gagging, or panic
Open the mouth and remove a visible object if safe
Avoid pushing an object deeper down the throat
Keep your dog as calm as you can
Get to emergency care if breathing is blocked
items.note: Take care, as a panicked dog may bite

items.text: Apply firm, steady pressure with a clean cloth
Hold pressure rather than lifting to look
Cover the wound loosely once bleeding slows
Keep your dog calm and limit movement
Go to a vet for deep or heavy bleeding
items.note: Heavy or spurting bleeding is an emergency, so go at once

items.text: Watch for heavy panting, drooling, or weakness
Move your dog to shade or air conditioning
Wet the coat with cool, not ice-cold, water
Offer small sips of water if your dog is alert
Get to a vet immediately, even if cooling helps
Check pads for cuts, splinters, or burns
Rinse a minor cut and apply gentle pressure if bleeding
Avoid moving a leg that may be broken
Limit walking and keep your dog still
See a vet for limping, swelling, or deep wounds
Support the body and avoid twisting an injured area
Use a board or blanket as a stretcher for a large dog
Keep your dog warm and calm during the trip
Call ahead so the clinic can prepare
Bring any packaging, medicines, or samples
This checklist is general information for owners, not veterinary advice; first aid does not replace professional care, so always consult a licensed veterinarian
items.note: In any emergency, contact your vet or an emergency animal hospital immediately

faq.q: How do I know if my dog is choking?
faq.a: Signs include pawing at the mouth, gagging, drooling, panic, or trouble breathing. Look inside the mouth and remove a visible object only if you can do so safely, then get emergency care right away.

faq.q: What should I do if my dog is bleeding?
faq.a: Apply firm, steady pressure with a clean cloth and keep it in place rather than checking repeatedly. Keep your dog calm and limit movement. Heavy or spurting bleeding is an emergency, so go to a vet at once.

faq.q: How do I recognize heatstroke in a dog?
faq.a: Watch for heavy panting, drooling, weakness, vomiting, bright red gums, or collapse. Move your dog to a cool, shaded place, offer small sips of water, and contact a vet immediately, as heatstroke is life-threatening.

faq.q: When should I call the vet for my dog?
faq.a: Call right away for breathing trouble, severe bleeding, collapse, seizures, suspected poisoning, bloating, or major trauma. When unsure, it is always safer to call your vet or an emergency animal hospital.

faq.q: Is this dog first aid checklist printable?
faq.a: Yes. Print it or download the PDF, keep it with your dog's emergency kit, and review it so the steps are familiar before you need them.
